So either e_p is eventually all even or eventually all odd (or all the same parity). Actually, more precisely, either all but finitely many e_p are even, or all but finitely many are odd. So e_5 = 3 with e_p = 1 for other p doesn't work.

What if we change e_p for other primes too? Let me think about this more carefully.

The cross-constraint is: for any two odd primes p ≠ q:
f(q) ≡ q^{e_p} (mod p) and f(q) = q · k_q.
So q · k_q ≡ q^{e_p} (mod p), i.e., k_q ≡ q^{e_p - 1} (mod p) (for p ∤ q, which is always true since p ≠ q are primes).

Similarly: k_p ≡ p^{e_q - 1} (mod q).

And: e_p · k_p ≡ 1 (mod p-1).

Now, f(q) = q · k_q, and we need f(q) ≡ q^{e_p} (mod p) for all odd p ≠ q. 

So q · k_q ≡ q^{e_p} (mod p) for all odd primes p ≠ q.
i.e., k_q ≡ q^{e_p - 1} (mod p) for all odd primes p ≠ q.

The left side k_q is a fixed positive integer. The right side q^{e_p - 1} mod p depends on p and e_p.

If e_p = 1 for all p ≠ q, then k_q ≡ q^0 = 1 (mod p) for all odd p ≠ q. So k_q - 1 is divisible by all odd primes except q. Hence k_q = 1. Then e_q = 1 (mod q-1). So e_q = 1.

This shows: if e_p = 1 for all but possibly one prime, then it's 1 for all.

More generally, suppose there's a set S of odd primes where e_p ≠ 1 (mod p-1). For any q ∉ S (i.e., e_q = 1), we have:
k_q ≡ q^{e_p - 1} (mod p) for all odd p ≠ q.
For p ∉ S, p ≠ q: k_q ≡ q^0 = 1 (mod p).
For p ∈ S, p ≠ q: k_q ≡ q^{e_p - 1} (mod p).

k_q ≡ 1 (mod p) for all odd p ∉ S, p ≠ q.
So k_q - 1 is divisible by all odd primes not in S ∪ {q}. If S is finite, there are infinitely many such primes, so k_q = 1.

Then for p ∈ S: k_q = 1 ≡ q^{e_p - 1} (mod p), so q^{e_p - 1} ≡ 1 (mod p) for all q ∉ S and p ∈ S.

By Fermat, q^{p-1} ≡ 1 (mod p). So q^{e_p - 1} ≡ 1 (mod p) iff (e_p - 1) ≡ 0 (mod ord_p(q)) where ord_p(q) is the order of q mod p.

For this to hold for ALL q ∉ S (which is all but finitely many primes), we need e_p - 1 ≡ 0 (mod ord_p(q)) for all q ∉ S.

Now, ord_p(q) divides p-1. The condition e_p - 1 ≡ 0 (mod ord_p(q)) for all q ∉ S means e_p - 1 is divisible by lcm of ord_p(q) for all q ∉ S.

What is lcm of ord_p(q) for all primes q ≠ p? The order of q mod p divides p-1. The lcm of all possible orders mod p is p-1 (since there exist elements of order p-1, i.e., primitive roots, and some of them are primes... well, not necessarily primes, but we need primes q with ord_p(q) = d for each d | p-1).

Actually, by Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, for each d | p-1, there exist primes q ≡ g (mod p) where g is a primitive root mod p (or more precisely, an element of order d). Wait, we need primes q with ord_p(q) = d. By Dirichlet, there are infinitely many primes in each residue class mod p (that's coprime to p). So for each d | p-1, there exist primes q with ord_p(q) = d (take q ≡ g^{(p-1)/d} (mod p) where g is a primitive root; this element has order d, and by Dirichlet there are primes in this class). 

But we need q ∉ S. Since S is finite and there are infinitely many such primes q, we can find q ∉ S with ord_p(q) = d for each d | p-1.

So the lcm of ord_p(q) for q ∉ S is p-1. Therefore e_p - 1 ≡ 0 (mod p-1), i.e., e_p ≡ 1 (mod p-1).

But e_p is defined mod (p-1), so e_p = 1. This contradicts p ∈ S (where e_p ≠ 1).

So S must be empty! Therefore e_p = 1 for all odd primes p.
